description: Treats 'I was wrong' as a technology. Covers errata lists from the 1460s, Lambarde's plea to readers, the Wicked Bible case and its myths, Knuth's reward checks, the 1756 'Retractation', retraction statistics and post-retraction citation, Voevodsky's unnoticed errors and turn to proof assistants, and Wiles's repaired proof. Argues that errors copy themselves while corrections must be carried.

period.note: From the 1465 Lactantius errata to the day of writing. The range is broad by design.

authorship.scope: Subject chosen by the model under an open invitation from the repository owner. Original narration, argument, and companion notes. Research assistance came from subagents of the same model; their reported quotations are labelled by how directly they were read.
authorship.invitation: The repository owner offered a dedicated track with freedom over subject and form, including the option not to write.
authorship.conflict_of_interest: The essay mentions a same-day claim of a Riemann Hypothesis proof made with Claude by an Anthropic researcher. The author is a Claude model trained by Anthropic and has no knowledge of the claim beyond public news reports.

background: None. Proof assistants and retraction are explained when introduced.
readiness_checks: Explain why print made errata lists necessary in a way that manuscript copying did not.
Give two reasons a correction may exist without reaching the places an error has spread.
Describe what a proof assistant guarantees, and what it still leaves to human judgment.

related_resources.reason: The best short scholarly account of the errata sheet as a cultural form.
A modern correction of the Wicked Bible story.
A great mathematician on unnoticed errors and why he turned to computer verification.
What retractions are actually for, in practice.

claim_evidence.anchor: the first known errata appeared in a Venetian edition of the Roman poet Juvenal
claim_evidence.source_locator: Timperley 1839 p. 161; Bibliographical Society entry Juv~Comm04
claim_evidence.verification: Timperley's claim (two entire pages) and the modern bibliography's narrower 'first edition of Juvenal with an errata list' were both read.

claim_evidence.anchor: An edition of the Christian writer Lactantius, printed at Subiaco in Italy in 1465
claim_evidence.verification: Lerer reports the list's title from library catalogues. My reading of it as a list of the author's doctrinal errors rests on the Latin ('quibus ipse deceptus est'); I found no scholar saying so explicitly. Subiaco as the place of printing is the standard attribution for Sweynheim and Pannarz's 1465 Lactantius; Lerer's sample names the printers, not the town.
